Easy.scenario: A test registers a new user, but fails on the second execution because the email 'testuser@email.com' is already taken.
Easy.q: What is the most basic strategy to resolve this data collision?
options: Append a unique timestamp or UUID to the email string during test execution
Manually delete the user from the DB before running tests
Catch the error and ignore it
Run tests synchronously
Easy.a: Append a unique timestamp or UUID to the email string during test execution
Easy.explanation: Generating dynamic, randomized identifiers ensures every test execution creates unique data, preventing state collisions.

Easy.code:
const user = require('./test-data.json');
test('login', async ({ page }) => { ... });
Easy.q: What is the limitation of using a static JSON file for test data?
options: It cannot contain dynamic identifiers, leading to collisions if tests run in parallel or mutate the data
JSON files cannot be read by Node.js
It makes the test run incredibly slow
Playwright blocks file system access
Easy.a: It cannot contain dynamic identifiers, leading to collisions if tests run in parallel or mutate the data
Easy.explanation: Static files share the exact same data payload across all tests. If one test mutates the user profile, the other tests using that static file will fail.

Medium.scenario: Your test suite needs realistic user names, addresses, and credit card numbers.
Medium.q: Which popular npm package is the industry standard for generating this realistic mock data on the fly?
options: Faker.js (@faker-js/faker)
Axios
Playwright-mock
Lodash
Medium.explanation: Faker generates highly realistic, randomized data for almost any category (names, dates, finances), making it perfect for dynamic test factories.

Medium.scenario: Your tests create database records using API calls in the `beforeEach` block.
Medium.q: What are the core requirements for managing this data lifecycle safely? (Select all that apply)
options: Store the generated record IDs in variables so they can be deleted later
Implement an `afterEach` or fixture teardown to clean up the records via API
Ensure the teardown block runs even if the test fails
Use direct SQL queries instead of the API
a: Store the generated record IDs in variables so they can be deleted later
Implement an `afterEach` or fixture teardown to clean up the records via API
Ensure the teardown block runs even if the test fails
Medium.explanation: Data cleanup requires tracking what was created and ensuring it gets deleted unconditionally. Using the API is generally preferred over direct SQL to ensure business logic triggers correctly.

Hard.scenario: You are testing a complex financial reporting dashboard. Creating the necessary 50,000 transaction records via API takes 2 minutes per test.
Hard.q: What is the most architecturally sound way to provide this data without destroying test execution speed?
options: Use a pre-seeded Database Dump / Snapshot that is rapidly loaded before the test suite begins
Use UI automation to create the records
Mock the network responses completely so the database isn't involved at all
Increase the test timeout to 3 minutes
Hard.a: Use a pre-seeded Database Dump / Snapshot that is rapidly loaded before the test suite begins
Hard.explanation: When data creation is overwhelmingly slow, relying on pre-seeded infrastructure (or Docker volumes) is the fastest approach for E2E tests. (Mocking is also valid for component tests, but reduces E2E confidence).

lessons.title: Module E: Network Mocking Deep Dive

Easy.scenario: You are testing a UI that displays a list of users fetched from `/api/users`. The backend server is currently down.
Easy.q: How can you run the test anyway?
options: Use page.route('**/api/users', route => route.fulfill({ json: mockUsers }))
Use page.waitForResponse and hardcode the timeout
You must wait for the server to come back up
Comment out the assertion
Easy.a: Use page.route('**/api/users', route => route.fulfill({ json: mockUsers }))
Easy.explanation: Mocking intercepts the request at the browser level and fulfills it instantly with your predefined JSON, removing backend dependency.

Easy.q: What happens if you run this line at the beginning of your test?
options: It blocks all network requests, so the page will fail to load CSS, JS, and API data
It mocks the entire internet successfully
It ignores CORS errors
It aborts the test execution
Easy.a: It blocks all network requests, so the page will fail to load CSS, JS, and API data
Easy.explanation: `route.abort()` completely kills the intercepted request. Routing `**/*` applies to literally everything the browser tries to fetch.

Medium.scenario: You want to mock a specific API response, but only if the request contains a specific header (e.g., `x-mock-test: true`).
Medium.q: How do you achieve this conditional routing?
options: Check the `route.request().headers()` inside the route callback. If the header exists, `fulfill()`. If not, call `route.fallback()` to let it go to the real server.
Pass the header requirement directly to the URL matching pattern string
It is impossible; you must mock all or nothing
Use page.evaluate to rewrite the headers
Medium.a: Check the `route.request().headers()` inside the route callback. If the header exists, `fulfill()`. If not, call `route.fallback()` to let it go to the real server.
Medium.explanation: The `route` object provides access to the full `request()`. `route.fallback()` is critical for conditional mocking, allowing unmatched requests to proceed normally.

Medium.scenario: You are testing an error boundary in your React application.
Medium.q: Which mocking strategies allow you to force the UI into an error state? (Select all that apply)
options: route.fulfill({ status: 500, body: 'Internal Server Error' })
route.abort('failed')
route.fallback()
route.continue()
Medium.explanation: You can either fulfill the request with an HTTP error code (simulating a backend crash) or abort it with an error string (simulating a network failure/DNS issue).

Hard.scenario: You want to test the real backend integration, but you need to modify one specific field in the JSON response as it comes back from the real server.
Hard.q: How do you implement this 'Modify Response' pattern?
options: Fetch the real response using `route.fetch()`, read the JSON, modify the field, and then call `route.fulfill({ response, json: modifiedJson })`
Call `route.continue()`, then intercept the response object and mutate it in memory
It cannot be done; you must either fully mock or fully hit the real server
Use a proxy server outside of Playwright
Hard.a: Fetch the real response using `route.fetch()`, read the JSON, modify the field, and then call `route.fulfill({ response, json: modifiedJson })`
Hard.explanation: This is a highly advanced pattern. `route.fetch()` fires the request to the real server and captures the response. You then mutate the payload and fulfill the route using the mutated data.

Easy.scenario: Your test fails with a `strict mode violation` error on `page.locator('.submit-btn').click()`.
Easy.q: What does this error fundamentally mean?
options: Playwright found more than one element matching the selector, so it refused to click because it doesn't know which one you meant
The element is hidden and cannot be clicked
The selector is invalid CSS
The page has not finished loading
Easy.a: Playwright found more than one element matching the selector, so it refused to click because it doesn't know which one you meant
Easy.explanation: Strict mode ensures test integrity. If a locator resolves to multiple nodes, Playwright throws an error rather than silently clicking the wrong one.

Easy.q: Why is resolving strict mode errors by using `.nth()` considered a code smell?
options: Because if a developer adds a new button earlier in the DOM, the index shifts and the test breaks. It is highly brittle.
Because nth() is deprecated
Because nth() only works on arrays
Because it is too slow
Easy.a: Because if a developer adds a new button earlier in the DOM, the index shifts and the test breaks. It is highly brittle.
Easy.explanation: Index-based location assumes the DOM structure never changes. Using text or ARIA roles is significantly more resilient.

Medium.scenario: Your test fails with `Element is intercepted by another element`.
Medium.q: What is the physical reality happening in the browser?
options: Playwright attempted to click the target, but an overlay, sticky header, or modal was covering the exact coordinates
The element has pointer-events: none
The element was deleted from the DOM just before the click
The element is outside the viewport
Medium.a: Playwright attempted to click the target, but an overlay, sticky header, or modal was covering the exact coordinates
Medium.explanation: Playwright calculates the X/Y coordinates of the element's center. If it determines that another element (like a spinner or modal) is physically layered on top, it throws an interception error.

Medium.scenario: You are dealing with an incredibly flaky third-party animation that causes interception errors.
Medium.q: Which strategies can you use to safely bypass this issue? (Select all that apply)
options: Use `click({ force: true })` to bypass the actionability checks and dispatch the event directly to the element
Use a web-first assertion to wait for the overlay to be hidden before clicking
Use `page.waitForTimeout(5000)`
Use `page.evaluate` to trigger the click via JavaScript
a: Use `click({ force: true })` to bypass the actionability checks and dispatch the event directly to the element
Use a web-first assertion to wait for the overlay to be hidden before clicking
Use `page.evaluate` to trigger the click via JavaScript
Medium.explanation: Forcing the click or using JS bypasses the visual check. The *best* approach is waiting for the overlay to disappear. Hardcoding timeouts is an anti-pattern.

Hard.scenario: A test randomly fails with a `TargetClosedError` or `Session closed` exception during navigation.
Hard.q: What architectural issue most commonly triggers this class of fatal error?
options: The test did not await a Promise correctly, causing the test block to finish and close the browser while an asynchronous operation was still running in the background
The internet connection dropped
The locator was wrong
The assertion failed
Hard.a: The test did not await a Promise correctly, causing the test block to finish and close the browser while an asynchronous operation was still running in the background
Hard.explanation: Floating promises cause extreme havoc. The runner thinks the test is done, tears down the context, and then the orphaned promise attempts to execute against a destroyed page.
